result: Zebrafish tolerate elevated temperatures (36°C) with high survival rates and minimal behavioral impairment. Adult survival was 100% for 10 days across all treatment groups, and larval survival exceeded 90% during the critical first 3 days. While swimming speed and vertical position increased at 36°C, social distance remained unchanged, swimming speed normalized after return to standard temperature, and olfactory discrimination learning was unaffected.
evaluation: Claims C6-C13 provide converging evidence from survival data, behavioral tracking, and learning assays demonstrating that zebrafish tolerate 36°C well. Statistical tests support behavioral claims (p<0.001 for speed/position, p=0.53 for social distance, p=0.76 for learning). The data establish that temperature elevation does not significantly compromise fish health or complex behaviors.

result: HSV1-mediated gene transfer efficiency in zebrafish is substantially enhanced by incubation at 36°C compared to 26°C. Reporter expression (DsRed) was observed in the olfactory bulb and retrogradely labeled neurons in the dorsal telencephalon, with substantially more neurons expressing DsRed at 36°C. Expression was first detected ~12 hours post-injection and remained stable for at least 10 days. Temperature shift experiments revealed that elevated temperature during the first 3 days post-injection is critical for enhanced expression.
evaluation: Claims C14-C22 demonstrate temperature-dependent enhancement of viral gene transfer through direct comparison of expression at different temperatures (C17, Figure 1B vs Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and temperature shift experiments (C20-C21). The time course data (C19) and stability observations provide additional support. The conclusion (C22) is well-justified by the experimental evidence.

result: HSV1-mediated gene transfer is effective throughout zebrafish development with temperature-dependent enhancement. In larvae, GFP expression increased with temperature (28.5°C < 32°C < 35°C) at 3 dpf, and strong expression was observed at 5 dpf and 14 dpf when maintained at 35°C. Retrograde labeling of motor neurons was achieved after muscle injection at 5 dpf.
evaluation: Claims C23-C27 provide experimental evidence across multiple developmental stages (3, 5, 7, 14 dpf) with appropriate sample sizes (N=3-14 fish per condition). The temperature dependence observed in larvae parallels adult findings. The retrograde tracing demonstration (C27) extends the utility of the approach. Conclusion C28 is appropriately supported.

result: HSV1 can be combined with the Gal4/UAS system for cell-type-specific gene expression in zebrafish. HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] showed no expression in wildtype fish but achieved 97.7±1.2% co-localization with GFP in GABAergic neurons of Tg[gad1b:Gal4; gad1b:GFP] cerebellum and 94.8±4.5% in dorsal telencephalon, with no expression in GFP-negative granule cells.
evaluation: Claims C29-C33 and C36 demonstrate high specificity through negative control (C29) and quantitative co-localization data (C31, C33) with low variability. The absence of expression in non-target cells (C32) confirms specificity. Sample sizes are adequate (N=3-5 fish). The conclusion (C37) is well-supported by the experimental evidence.

result: Viral labeling revealed that the dorsal telencephalon contains specific long-range projections of GABAergic neurons, with neurites arborizing extensively in the lateral pallium while sparing regions immediately adjacent to the gad1b-positive cluster.
evaluation: Claims C34-C35 describe a novel anatomical finding supported by imaging data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). The spatial pattern of mCherry-expressing neurites provides direct evidence for the inference about specific long-range GABAergic projections. This is a valid anatomical observation enabled by the viral tracing method.

result: HSV1/Gal4/UAS intersectional targeting achieves high specificity and efficiency for sparse neuronal populations. Selective expression was achieved in catecholaminergic neurons of the locus coeruleus (N=4 fish) and in OB-projecting neurons of the dorsal telencephalon. The Gal4/UAS approach yielded similar numbers of labeled neurons as the one-component approach.
evaluation: Claims C38-C40 demonstrate successful intersectional targeting in two different sparse populations with appropriate controls. The quantitative comparison (C40, Figure 2F) shows equivalent efficiency between approaches. The conclusion (C41) about high efficiency and low leakiness is supported by the experimental data.

result: Multiple transgenes can be co-expressed in the same neurons through either co-packaging (89.5±8.7% co-expression) or co-injection (84.3±6.0% co-expression) of separate viruses, even when overall expression is sparse.
evaluation: Claims C42-C43 provide quantitative data showing high co-expression rates for both strategies (N=3 fish each). The similar rates between co-packaging and co-injection are notable and well-documented. The conclusion (C44) is appropriately supported by the data.

result: Virally transduced neurons expressing GCaMP6f and Chrimson-tdTomato are functional and responsive to optogenetic stimulation, with calcium transients increasing in amplitude with light intensity (500ms pulses, 1.3-8.6 mW).
evaluation: Claims C45-C46 demonstrate functional expression through optogenetic stimulation and calcium imaging (N=21 neurons from one fish, Figure 2—figure supplement 3). The dose-response relationship supports neuronal functionality. However, the single-fish sample limits generalizability.

result: Expression of tetanus toxin light chain (TeNT-GFP) in cerebellar GABAergic neurons via HSV1 caused abnormal swimming behavior including slow swimming, circular trajectories, and altered vertical positioning, while control fish injected with HSV1[UAS:GFP] swam normally.
evaluation: Claims C47-C48 describe clear behavioral phenotypes with appropriate controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 4). However, C49 acknowledges that the mechanism is uncertain and requires further experiments. The behavioral effects are consistent with TeNT function but causality is not definitively established. Sample sizes are not provided for this experiment.

result: A collection of 26 different HSV1 vectors has been assembled for zebrafish applications, including 15 with LTCMV promoter-driven expression and 11 with UAS-dependent expression for use with the Gal4/UAS system.
evaluation: Claims C51-C53 describe the viral toolbox with documentation in Figure 2—source data 1 file1. This is a straightforward descriptive result about resource availability. The collection represents a significant methodological contribution to the field.

result: EnvA-RVΔG-GFP infection of zebrafish neurons requires TVA expression and is substantially more efficient at 36°C than at 26°C. No expression was observed in wildtype fish at 36°C, but efficient and selective infection occurred in Tg[gad1b:Gal4; UAS:TVA-mCherry] fish at 36°C after 6 days, with no infection at 26°C or when temperature was raised from 26°C to 36°C 3 days post-injection.
evaluation: Claims C60-C63 establish TVA-dependence through negative control (C60) and demonstrate temperature-dependence through systematic comparison (C61, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The temperature shift experiment (C61) confirms that elevated temperature must be present during initial infection. The conclusions (C62-C63) are well-supported.

result: RNA sequencing of RVΔG-infected neurons revealed 522 downregulated and 27 upregulated genes (of 19,819 analyzed), with stress and cell death markers occurring at average or below-average frequencies. The 65 significantly associated GO terms were primarily related to immune responses, with GO terms for stress, cell death, electrophysiological properties, or synapses being rare or absent.
evaluation: Claims C64-C68 present comprehensive transcriptomic analysis with appropriate statistical thresholds (abs(logFC)>3, logCPM>3, FDR<0.05). The GO term analysis (C67-C68) supports the interpretation that changes reflect immune response rather than cellular stress (C69-C70). However, the interpretation would benefit from comparison to other viral infections or stress conditions.

result: RVΔG-infected neurons showed no obvious differences in odor-evoked calcium responses compared to uninfected neurons in the same fish, with similar time courses and amplitude distributions (N=1293 infected and N=559 uninfected neurons from 4 fish).
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 provide functional evidence for lack of toxicity through direct comparison of infected and uninfected neurons within the same animals (Figure 3E-G). The large sample size and within-animal control design strengthen the conclusion. This complements the transcriptomic data.

result: To enhance glycoprotein expression for transneuronal spread, codon usage was optimized for zebrafish (zoSADG) and TVA/zoSADG were expressed using HSV1 rather than transgenics, as viral vectors typically achieve higher expression levels.
evaluation: Claims C74-C75 describe methodological optimizations with rationale supported by citation (C75, Zou et al., 2014). These are reasonable design choices based on established principles, though direct comparison of expression levels is not shown.

result: Trans-complementation with zoSADG in starter cells promoted transneuronal spread of rabies virus in the cerebellum. Without glycoprotein, GFP expression was restricted to starter neurons with no expression in the inferior olive. With zoSADG, starter neuron numbers declined over 10 days while GFP+ neurons increased steeply between 6-10 days, appearing in granule cells and the contralateral inferior olive.
evaluation: Claims C78-C86 provide systematic comparison of conditions with and without glycoprotein complementation (Figure 4B-D). The time course (C80-C81) and spatial distribution (C83-C85) data support transneuronal spread. The observation that delayed rabies injection doesn't increase labeling (C82) is consistent with rodent studies. The conclusion (C86) is well-supported.

result: The convergence index for transneuronal viral transfer from inferior olive to Purkinje neurons was 1.00±0.95 (N=4 fish), comparable to values reported in mammals.
evaluation: Claims C87-C88 provide quantitative assessment using an established metric with comparison to mammalian studies (Kim et al., 2016). The convergence index provides a benchmark for efficiency, though the authors acknowledge it doesn't reflect true convergence due to starter cell loss. The comparison to mammals is appropriate.

result: EnvA-RVΔG selectively infects TVA-expressing neurons and undergoes monosynaptic retrograde transneuronal transfer when complemented with zoSADG in the telencephalon. Without zoSADG, GFP was restricted to starter neurons; with zoSADG, widespread GFP expression occurred including mitral cells in the OB. Convergence indices were 0.70±0.21 for GABAergic starters (N=5) and 1.31±1.20 for glutamatergic starters (N=4).
evaluation: Claims C90-C98 replicate the cerebellar findings in a different circuit with both GABAergic and glutamatergic starter populations. The vglut1 expression pattern (C94) provides evidence that OB labeling results from transneuronal spread rather than direct infection (C95). Convergence indices (C96-C97) are consistent with the cerebellar data. The conclusion (C98) is well-supported.

result: Glycoprotein-dependent retrograde transneuronal transfer occurs in zebrafish larvae. In Tg[gad1b:Gal4; UAS:TVA-mCherry] fish at 10 dpf, GFP expression was restricted to mCherry+ neurons at the spinal cord injection site without zoSADG, but with zoSADG, GFP expression appeared throughout the spinal cord and brainstem in neurons that typically did not co-express mCherry.
evaluation: Claims C99-C102 demonstrate that transneuronal tracing works at larval stages (Figure 5A-B), extending the utility of the approach. The pattern of GFP expression (C100-C101) is consistent with transneuronal spread. The conclusion (C102) is appropriately supported.

result: Temperature affects viral gene expression by modulating the infection process rather than through indirect effects like cell proliferation. A transient temperature shift around the time of injection is sufficient for high expression, allowing fish to be returned to standard temperature days before experiments, minimizing effects on subsequent activity measurements or behavioral analyses.
evaluation: Claims C103-C107 provide mechanistic interpretation and practical implications of the temperature findings. The temperature shift experiments (C20-C21) support C104-C105. The behavioral data (C8-C13) support C107. However, C104 acknowledges uncertainty about the precise mechanism, and C103 is somewhat speculative.

result: HSV1 can be combined with the Gal4/UAS system for two-component gene expression without obvious leakiness, enabling intersectional targeting strategies. Expression can be directed to specific neurons by injecting HSV1 with UAS-dependent inserts into existing Gal4 driver lines. Viral delivery may overcome epigenetic silencing of UAS elements observed in some transgenic lines.
evaluation: Claims C108-C113 summarize the intersectional targeting capabilities demonstrated throughout the paper. C108 is supported by multiple experiments (C29-C41). C109-C110 describe the methodological approach. C111-C112 are speculative but supported by citations about epigenetic silencing (Akitake et al., 2011; Goll et al., 2009). C113 is an appropriate concluding statement.

result: Enhanced transneuronal spread compared to previous zebrafish studies (Dohaku et al., 2019) resulted from multiple factors including temperature adjustment (important but insufficient alone, as temperature difference was only 1.5°C), codon optimization, viral gene delivery, and possibly experimental schedule differences.
evaluation: Claims C114-C116 provide comparative analysis with appropriate citation. The reasoning about multiple contributing factors (C115-C116) is sound given the small temperature difference. However, C116 is somewhat speculative as direct comparisons of individual factors were not performed.

result: Starter neurons expressing glycoprotein G disappeared during the first 10 days after virus injection, while neurons infected with RVΔG alone did not substantially decline. Transcriptional profiling showed RVΔG primarily changed immunity-related gene expression, suggesting transneuronally labeled neurons remain physiologically functional for up to 10 days despite starter neuron loss, consistent with rodent observations.
evaluation: Claims C119-C123 integrate time-course data (C119-C120), transcriptomics (C121), and functional imaging (C71-C72) to support the conclusion about a functional time window (C122-C123). The comparison to rodent studies (C123, multiple citations) strengthens the interpretation. The evidence converges well.

result: Transneuronal spread of rabies virus was glycoprotein-dependent and labeled substantial numbers of presynaptic neurons in both adult and larval zebrafish. Convergence ratios were similar to rodents despite smaller zebrafish neurons that likely receive fewer synaptic inputs, suggesting transneuronal tracing efficiency is in the same range as rodents.
evaluation: Claims C124-C126 provide summary conclusions supported by the cerebellar (C78-C88), telencephalic (C90-C98), and larval (C99-C102) experiments. The comparison to rodents (C125-C126) is appropriate given the convergence index data, though C126 acknowledges difficulty in quantitative comparison.

result: Rabies-based transneuronal tracers are promising tools for structural and functional dissection of neuronal circuitry in zebrafish. The small size of zebrafish facilitates combining circuit tracing with high-resolution imaging of neuronal activity. Anterograde transneuronal tracing using VSVs may complement retrograde rabies tracing.
evaluation: Claims C128-C131 provide appropriate concluding statements about the utility and future directions of the methods. C128-C129 are supported by the experimental results. C130 is a valid statement about zebrafish advantages. C131 is supported by citations to VSV studies (Kler et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019; Mundell et al., 2015).

result: Viral gene transfer will be most useful for analyzing neuronal circuit structure and function in juvenile or adult zebrafish, which exhibit richer behavioral repertoires than larvae but face challenges with declining transgene expression. Some brain areas remain optically accessible at these stages, enabling combination of viral tools with genetic and optical approaches for novel experimental opportunities.
evaluation: Claims C133-C140 provide appropriate discussion of applications and limitations. C133-C134 acknowledge temporal resolution limits while identifying optimal applications. C136-C137 are supported by citations about behavior and transgene expression. C139 is supported by citation (Huang et al., 2020). The conclusions are reasonable and well-supported.

result: AAVs fail to infect zebrafish brain neurons, while HSV1 can infect zebrafish neurons both locally and retrogradely without obvious cytotoxicity.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 cite established prior work (Zhu et al., 2009; Zou et al., 2014) to provide context for the current study. These are appropriately cited background claims that justify the focus on HSV1.

result: Background knowledge claims about zebrafish neuroanatomy, rabies virus methodology, and established principles in the field.
evaluation: These claims (C16, C54-C57, C73, C76-C77, C89, C109, C117-C118, C127, C129-C130) represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations or are standard anatomical/methodological descriptions. They provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study.
